lead: This unit covers the electronics between a vehicle's sensing and its actions: the semiconductor components and microcontrollers inside the ECU, the sensors that measure air, crank position, throttle, temperature, oxygen, knock and battery state, and the actuators and electric motors that carry out its commands. After it you can trace a signal from a sensing element through the ECU to an actuator and work the numbers at each step.
about: The unit starts inside the ECU, with semiconductor components and the microcontroller, then follows the signal path: sensor basics and signal conditioning, air flow and manifold pressure, crankshaft position, Hall, reluctance and optical sensing, throttle and temperature, exhaust oxygen, and knock, acceleration and torque. It then turns to the output side: solenoids, relays and stepper motors, fluid-mechanical actuators, and the electrical machines in a vehicle with their duty ratings. It ends with battery current, voltage and state-of-charge sensing, which only a few universities teach.

chapters.idea: A sensor converts a physical quantity into an electrical signal, and signal conditioning makes that signal usable by the ECU.
chapters.depth: Define sensor, transducer, actuator, measured variable, range, span, sensitivity, resolution, accuracy, linearity, hysteresis, drift and response time. Classify active and passive, analog and digital, contact and non-contact, absolute and relative sensors. Cover resistive, capacitive, inductive, piezoelectric, thermoelectric, Hall and MEMS sensing elements. Explain signal conditioning: bridge, amplifier, filter, isolation, linearisation, cold-junction compensation, sample-and-hold and ADC. Some syllabi call this 'automotive variables and measured quantities' and list position, speed, acceleration, force, torque, flow, gas concentration and temperature. Use one table to map quantity to common sensor.

figure.title: Sensor signal path
figure.aria: Block diagram from physical quantity to sensing element to signal conditioning to ADC to ECU.

chapters.example: A coolant thermistor is in a 5 V divider with a 1 kΩ fixed resistor. At 25 °C its resistance is 2 kΩ; at 80 °C it is 0.5 kΩ. Find the divider output at both temperatures and the 10-bit ADC counts for a 0–5 V ADC. Answer: V=5R/(R+1k) gives 3.333 V and 1.667 V; counts=round(1023V/5) give 682 and 341.
chapters.trap: Do not treat ADC count as the physical value. The thermistor curve is nonlinear, so convert and linearise; also account for self-heating and reference tolerance.
chapters.prereq: Basic electrical circuits: voltage divider, Ohm's law; Unit 1 battery voltage and power supply ideas.
chapters.leave: Detailed ECU control modes to Unit 4; CAN and diagnostics to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Air flow and manifold pressure sensors measure the air charge entering the engine, which sets fuel quantity.
chapters.depth: Cover MAF: vane, hot-wire, hot-film and Karman vortex. Cover MAP: strain-gauge diaphragm, capacitive and piezoresistive. Compare speed-density and mass-air methods. Define volumetric efficiency, manifold absolute pressure, barometric pressure and intake air temperature compensation. Explain hot-wire bridge and burn-off; Karman vortex frequency; strain-gauge bridge and signal conditioning. Some syllabi call MAP a strain gauge pressure sensor and MAF an air flow meter.

figure.aria: Line graph of MAP sensor output voltage versus manifold absolute pressure, 0.5 V at 20 kPa to 4.5 V at 100 kPa.

chapters.example: A 1.6 L four-stroke engine at 3000 rpm has MAP 60 kPa, volumetric efficiency 0.90 and intake temperature 300 K. Take R=287 J/(kg·K). Estimate air mass flow. Answer: N=50 rev/s; air per second = η_v P_man V_d (N/2)/(R T) = 0.90×60000×0.0016×25/(287×300)=0.0251 kg/s = 25.1 g/s.
chapters.trap: Do not use rpm directly; a four-stroke engine has one intake stroke per two revolutions. MAF is direct mass flow; MAP needs speed, displacement, volumetric efficiency and temperature.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 signal conditioning; basic engine displacement and gas law; Unit 4 fuel control for mixture use.
chapters.leave: Fuel injection pulse calculation and emission control to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Crankshaft position and speed sensors give the ECU the piston position and engine speed needed for ignition and fuel timing.
chapters.depth: Cover CKP and CMP, inductive or variable-reluctance, Hall, optical and magnetoresistive types. Cover toothed wheels such as 60-2 and 36-1, missing-tooth synchronisation, edge detection, speed from pulse period, timing sensor for ignition and fuel delivery, angular position versus angular speed. Include signal amplitude versus speed for VR and digital output for Hall. Some syllabi say engine crankshaft angular position sensor, engine angular speed sensor and timing sensor.

figure.aria: Timeline at 3000 rpm of crank tooth pulses every 333 µs, with a three-period missing-tooth gap and an ECU sync pulse after it.

chapters.example: A 60-2 crank wheel turns at 3000 rpm. Find the normal tooth period and the missing-tooth gap. Answer: 3000 rpm = 50 rev/s; one revolution = 20 ms; 60 slots = 0.333 ms per tooth; the two missing teeth produce a gap of 3×0.333=1.00 ms between the last tooth and the next tooth.
chapters.trap: Do not call the missing-tooth gap two periods; it is three periods for a 60-2 wheel. At low speed a VR sensor may not produce enough voltage, so the ECU may use a Hall sensor.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 signal conditioning; basic angular motion and frequency.
chapters.leave: Ignition coil and injector drivers to 3.8 and Unit 2; detailed ignition timing maps to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Hall, magnetic reluctance and optical sensors convert position or rotation into a voltage or pulse without contact.
chapters.depth: Explain Hall effect: V_H = K_H I B, with I current, B flux density and K_H a coefficient. Cover Hall switches and latches, magnetoresistive sensors, variable-reluctance or inductive sensors with AC output whose amplitude and frequency rise with speed, and optical slotted or vane sensors with LED and phototransistor. Compare contact and non-contact, digital and analog, speed range and dirt sensitivity. Include optical crankshaft position sensing. Some syllabi call magnetic reluctance 'variable reluctance' and optical 'optoelectronic'.

figure.title: Hall sensor chain
figure.aria: Block diagram from Hall element to amplifier to Schmitt trigger to ECU.

chapters.example: A Hall plate has current I=10 mA, thickness t=0.5 mm, carrier density n=1×10²² m⁻³, and flux density B=0.1 T. Take q=1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C. Find V_H. Answer: V_H = I B/(n q t) = 0.01×0.1/(1×10²²×1.6×10⁻¹⁹×0.0005) = 1.25 mV; an amplifier raises this to a logic level.
chapters.trap: A VR sensor is not a Hall sensor: its output is an AC voltage that depends on speed, so it needs a threshold and often a zero-crossing detector. A Hall sensor needs a supply and gives a digital signal.
chapters.prereq: 3.3 crank position; magnetic field and induction basics.
chapters.leave: Detailed ECU decoding to 3.3; LIDAR ranging to 3.7.

chapters.idea: Throttle position and temperature sensors tell the ECU the driver demand and the thermal state of the engine, intake and cabin.
chapters.depth: Cover potentiometric and contactless TPS, idle and wide-open-throttle switches, and pedal position redundancy. Cover coolant temperature (ECT) and intake air temperature (IAT) NTC thermistors, divider circuits and table or Steinhart-Hart linearisation. Include thermistors for battery and onboard thermal sensing, humidity and air-quality sensors, and integration of cabin temperature, humidity, sun load and air-quality signals into climate control. Some syllabi call TPS throttle angle sensor and ECT coolant sensor.

figure.aria: Line graph of throttle position sensor voltage versus throttle percent, 0.5 V at 0% and 4.5 V at 100%.

chapters.example: A 5 V TPS is linear: 0.5 V at 0% throttle and 4.5 V at 100%. Find the voltage at 30% and the 10-bit ADC count for a 0–5 V ADC. Answer: V=0.5+0.04×30=1.70 V; count=round(1023×1.70/5)=348.
chapters.trap: A thermistor is nonlinear; do not use a straight-line conversion. Check the pull-up resistor and supply because a small reference error shifts the temperature reading. TPS redundancy is checked by the ECU: two tracks must agree.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 signal conditioning; voltage divider; 3.4 contactless sensing.
chapters.leave: Cabin actuator control details to 3.8; engine fuel maps to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: The exhaust gas oxygen sensor measures oxygen in exhaust and lets the ECU keep the air-fuel ratio near stoichiometric or a target lambda.
chapters.depth: Cover narrowband zirconia EGO sensor: Nernst principle, 0.1–0.9 V switching around λ=1, heated sensor, thimble and planar types. Cover wideband UEGO with pump cell and linear output, and titania sensors. Define λ, stoichiometric AFR 14.7:1 for petrol, rich and lean, closed-loop fuel trim. Explain desirable and switching characteristics: fast light-off, high sensitivity, low hysteresis, poison resistance and heater control. Some syllabi call it lambda sensor or HEGO.

figure.aria: Line graph of narrowband EGO voltage against lambda, switching sharply near lambda equal to one.

chapters.example: A petrol engine has stoichiometric AFR 14.7:1. A narrowband EGO reads 15.4:1. Find λ and state whether the output is high or low. Answer: λ=15.4/14.7=1.048, so the mixture is lean; a narrowband sensor output is low, about 0.1 V, not a proportional 0.048 reading.
chapters.trap: Do not read a narrowband EGO voltage as a linear AFR; it switches. A cold sensor does not work, so the heater and light-off time matter. Lead and silicone poisoning reduce response.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 signal conditioning; Unit 4 combustion and fuel control; Chapter 2 air charge.
chapters.leave: Three-way catalyst and emission norms to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Knock, acceleration, torque and angular-rate sensors measure mechanical vibration and motion so the ECU can protect the engine and stabilise the vehicle.
chapters.depth: Cover piezoelectric knock sensor and resonant frequency band roughly 5–15 kHz, charge amplifier, band-pass filter, window and threshold. Cover MEMS accelerometers with capacitive comb, angular-rate gyroscopes, torque sensors using strain gauge, magnetoelastic or SAW methods, LIDAR time-of-flight ranging and flex-fuel sensors using dielectric or fuel composition measurement. Include force, vibrational and acceleration measurement for crash and ESP use. Some syllabi list lateral acceleration and angular rate sensor.

figure.title: Knock signal path
figure.aria: Block diagram from knock vibration to piezo element to charge amplifier to band-pass filter to rectifier to ECU.

chapters.example: A piezoelectric knock sensor has charge sensitivity d=2 pC/N. A knock force of 50 N produces charge q=dF=100 pC. With a charge amplifier feedback capacitor C_f=1000 pF, find output voltage. Answer: V=q/C_f=100×10⁻¹²/1000×10⁻¹²=0.10 V.
chapters.trap: Do not amplify all engine noise: knock detection uses a band-pass filter around the knock frequency and a crank-angle window. A gyroscope measures angular rate, not angle; integration drifts.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 signal conditioning; 3.4 Hall and optical position sensing; basic mechanics.
chapters.leave: ESP and airbag algorithms to Unit 5; ADAS and detailed LIDAR use to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Actuators convert ECU electrical commands into mechanical action using solenoids, relays, stepper motors and motor drives.
chapters.depth: Cover solenoid force and current, pull-in and hold current, freewheeling diode, low-side and high-side drivers, and PWM current control. Cover relays and contactors, H-bridge DC motor drive, stepper motor full-step, half-step and microstep operation, step angle and torque-speed limits. Apply to fuel injectors, EGR valves, variable valve timing, electric motor actuators, ignition coil drivers and vacuum-operated actuators. Some syllabi call these output devices. Keep ignition combustion details to Unit 2 and fuel maps to Unit 4.

figure.title: Actuator drive
figure.aria: Block diagram from ECU to driver to solenoid to valve.

chapters.example: A stepper motor has a 1.8° step angle. The ECU sends 400 steps in 0.8 s. Find the total angle, revolutions and average speed. Answer: angle=400×1.8=720°=2 rev; speed=2/0.8=2.5 rev/s=150 rpm.
chapters.trap: A stepper motor is open-loop and can lose steps if the load torque is too high. A relay coil needs a flyback diode; without it the driver transistor can be damaged.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 signal conditioning; basic transistors, diodes and magnetic circuits; Unit 2 ignition coil driver.
chapters.leave: Fuel injection quantity and EGR strategy to Unit 4; CAN commands to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Battery current and voltage sensing let the BMS estimate state of charge, state of health and state of function.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this chapter, so keep it short. Cover shunt resistor and Hall current sensors, isolated voltage measurement, voltage divider and ADC, battery modules, regenerative braking current direction, and BMS sensors for SOC, SOH and SOF. Give coulomb counting and open-circuit-voltage reset. Mention thermistors and thermal sensing from 3.5. Do not derive electrochemical models.

figure.title: Battery sensing
figure.aria: Block diagram from battery to shunt to amplifier to ADC to BMS.

chapters.example: A 50 Ah battery starts at SOC 80%. It discharges at 10 A for 30 min. Find the charge removed and the new SOC by coulomb counting. Answer: charge=10×0.5=5 Ah; SOC drop=5/50=10%; new SOC=80−10=70%.
chapters.trap: Coulomb counting drifts because current offset and capacity fade accumulate; reset with OCV after rest. A shunt needs a Kelvin connection and temperature compensation.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 signal conditioning; 3.5 thermistors; Unit 1 battery ratings and charging.
chapters.leave: Battery chemistry and charging circuits to Unit 1; BMS communication and diagnostics to Unit 6.
